summary: This unit teaches you to monitor the performance of individuals and teams in a Jamaican public body or business and to give feedback that improves it. You will learn to agree clear targets and standards, choose monitoring methods, use simple data, avoid bias, give and receive feedback, recognise good work, deal with performance gaps fairly, keep secure records and review whether your monitoring system works.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers in ministries, agencies, municipal corporations, schools, hotels and businesses who are responsible for the work of others. **Monitoring performance** means checking, regularly and fairly, how well people and teams are doing against agreed expectations. **Feedback** means telling people what you have seen, so that good work continues and weak work improves.

Monitoring is not spying and it is not an annual event. Done well, it is open, planned and linked to targets that people understand. Its purpose is to help the team deliver its work plan, to spot problems early and to treat every officer fairly. This kit takes you through the work in the order a manager does it: agree expectations, collect evidence, judge fairly, give feedback, recognise good work, close gaps, record and review.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your unit
rows: Set duties, standards and targets with each officer, and link them to the unit's work plan and the agency's goals.
Pick key performance indicators (KPIs) and a mix of evidence: records, observation, samples, client views.
Work out percentages, averages and progress against target; check the figures before you act on them.
Use the same standards for everyone, keep dated notes and know the common rating errors.
Plan feedback, give it privately, early and specifically, listen, agree actions, and welcome feedback on your own work.
Praise specifically and use low-cost ways to reward effort, including team recognition.
Find the cause, coach, agree an improvement plan, follow formal procedure when needed and support staff in difficulty.
Keep records and review the system
Write short factual notes, store them securely, and improve the monitoring forms and routines.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper on expectations, methods, data, bias, feedback, gaps and records.
A written paper with short answers (exact terms such as SMART, KPI, SBI, GROW, halo effect) and longer answers in which you plan monitoring or a feedback meeting.
Group practical tasks: building a monitoring plan and analysing a month of team data, and role-playing feedback meetings with agreed actions.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact terms and for simple sums. Learn the terms in the Revision section and practise the percentage and average sums in this kit.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Agreeing expectations: standards, targets and KPIs

blocks.p: You cannot monitor fairly until people know what is expected. Your first task, when you take over a team or when a work year starts, is to **agree expectations** with each officer. These come from the job description, the unit's work plan and the agency's corporate plan.

head: Term
Meaning
Example in a municipal corporation
rows: A task that is part of the job
A stated level of quality, quantity or time for a task
Each inspection report is complete, accurate and filed within two working days
A specific result to be reached by a date
A measure used to track progress towards an important target
Percentage of inspections completed within five working days of the request
A starting measurement, taken so that later results can be compared with it
Last year, 62% of inspections met the five-day limit

blocks.p: A standard says **how well**; a target says **how much by when**. A KPI is the number you watch. A baseline tells you where you started, so you can tell whether things are improving.
A good target is **SMART**: **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant and **T**ime-bound. Compare two versions of the same target.

head: Weak target
SMART version
What was fixed
rows: "File all incoming letters within two working days, from 1 March."
"Reply to 90% of written complaints within 10 working days this quarter."
A number, a limit and a period
"Cut the errors found in file checks from 8 in every 100 files to 4 by the end of June."
A starting point, a target and a date

blocks.p: A target must also be **achievable**. A target of 100% on every measure, with no allowance for leave, sick days or system breakdowns, sets people up to fail. It must be **relevant**: linked to the unit's work plan, not just easy to count.

blocks.h: Why agree targets with the officer

ul: Officers are more committed to targets they helped to shape.
They can tell you early if a target is unrealistic or if they need a resource or training.
Both sides know the standard, so later feedback is not a surprise.
Targets can be written into the performance appraisal form that many public bodies use.

blocks.p: Agreed does not mean the officer can change the target alone. The manager is accountable for the unit's results, so the final targets must still fit the work plan. Where targets are not agreed, explain the reason clearly.

blocks.h: Choosing measures: avoid a single number

blocks.p: A single measure can distort behaviour. If a roads unit is judged only on the number of potholes filled, crews may rush and fill them badly. Use a **balanced set** of measures:

head: Type of measure
What it shows
Example
rows: Percentage of files with no errors on checking
Share of cases closed within the set time
Satisfaction score from a short survey

blocks.note: Choose a few measures that matter, not many that are easy to count. If nobody uses a measure, stop collecting it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Monitoring should be **built into normal work routines** so that problems are found and dealt with early, not discovered at the yearly appraisal. It should be **open** (people know what is checked and why), **planned** (set dates and methods) and **linked to agreed targets**.

blocks.h: Methods and when to use them

head: Method
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Records may be incomplete or entered late
The sample must be fair, for example chosen at random
How officers deal with clients and follow procedures
People may behave differently when watched; use a checklist and tell them in advance
Use a checklist and a sample, not only the worst calls
Service as the public sees it
Complaints alone give a negative picture
Keep them regular, not only when something goes wrong

blocks.p: The fairest picture comes from a **mix of evidence**. For a building inspector, for example, use inspection records (quantity and time), a quality check of a sample of reports, and feedback from applicants.

flow: Confirm the unit's goals and each officer's agreed targets
Choose the KPIs and the evidence for each one
Set the timetable: weekly, monthly and quarterly checks
Decide who collects each item and who analyses it
Tell the team what will be checked and why
Review the results regularly and share them
Act: give feedback, recognise good work, deal with gaps

blocks.p: Managers must be able to work out simple results and check them twice. Learn these four sums.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: Add the values, divide by how many
Cases took 4, 6, 8, 5 and 7 days: total 30 ÷ 5 = 6 days
Expected so far = target ÷ months × months passed
Target 900 in 3 months; after 2 months expect 600; if 520 done, the team is 80 behind

blocks.p: **Average** hides differences. An average of 6 days could be five cases at 6 days, or four fast ones and one very slow one. Look also at the longest and shortest times.

ul: **Check the data first.** A fall of 15% in one month may come from missing records, a system failure, public holidays or a change in the type of cases, not from poor effort.
**Compare like with like.** An officer who closes far more cases than others may be taking easy cases, or skipping checks. Look at the type and quality of cases before you praise or blame.
**Look for trends,** not single months.
**Ask what the figures do not show,** for example client comments or an officer's help to colleagues.
**Use the baseline** to see whether things have improved.

blocks.note: Data tells you where to look and what to ask. It does not give the answer by itself. Talk to the officer before you judge.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: When the process, not the person, is the problem

blocks.p: Suppose a team misses its target three months in a row although every officer is busy. Files may wait days between steps: waiting for a signature, a courier or a second check. Then the likely cause is the **way work flows through the process**, not laziness. Map the steps, measure the waiting time at each one, and fix the delay. Blaming individuals would be unfair and would not solve it.
Every judgement of performance must rest on **evidence** and on the **same agreed standards for every officer**. Managers are human, so several common rating errors creep in.

head: Error
What happens
How to avoid it
rows: One strong point, such as good public speaking, colours the whole rating
Rate each criterion separately, with evidence
One weak point leads to low ratings in everything
Same: rate each target on its own evidence
Recent events outweigh the rest of the review period
Keep dated notes through the year
Rating everyone in the middle to avoid difficult conversations
Use clear definitions for each rating level
Rating everyone too high, or too low
Compare with the standard, not with colleagues
Favouring people who share your background or views
Check ratings against evidence; ask a second person to review
Judging by age, gender, parish, religion or disability

ul: Judge every officer against the **same agreed standards**.
Keep **short, dated notes** all year: both good and poor performance.
Collect evidence from more than one source.
Separate the person from the performance: describe the work, not the character.
Ask a second manager to review ratings, especially where they affect pay, promotion or discipline.
Be aware of your own preferences, and use a checklist.

blocks.note: Treating an officer less fairly because of religion, gender, age, disability or similar personal factors is unfair, goes against public service rules and may break the law. If in doubt, ask the human resource unit.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Feedback** is information about performance, given so that the person can continue what works and change what does not. It may be **informal** (a quick word after a client meeting) or **formal** (a planned review meeting, which is recorded). Use both: informal feedback is quick and keeps small problems small; formal feedback gives a record and a proper discussion.

head: Good feedback is...
Because...
rows: It is most useful soon after the work, while it is fresh in mind
"In two of today's files the hearing date was missing" can be acted on; "your files are sloppy" cannot
It describes what was done, not what kind of person the officer is
It says what to keep doing as well as what to change
Correction in front of colleagues causes shame and defensiveness
The officer is asked for views and ideas
Without actions and a follow-up date, nothing changes

blocks.p: The **situation-behaviour-impact (SBI)** model keeps feedback factual.

head: Step
What you do
Example
rows: "In Tuesday's client meeting at the Falmouth office..."
Describe what you saw or heard, without judging
"...you explained each step of the process and checked that the client understood."
Say what effect it had on people or the work
"The client completed the form correctly and did not need to return."

blocks.p: SBI works for praise and for correction. For corrective feedback, finish by asking: "How do you see it?" and "What could we do differently?"

blocks.h: Planning and holding a feedback meeting

flow: Check the facts: dates, figures, the exact problem and its effect
Note what the officer does well, and think about possible causes
Choose a private place and a calm time, and tell the officer the purpose
Open by stating the purpose and the facts, using SBI
Ask for the officer's view and listen without interrupting
Agree what will change, what support you will give and the date to review
Write a short note of the meeting and follow up

blocks.h: Asking questions that make people reflect

blocks.p: Questions such as "How do you think the site visit went, and what would you change?" invite the officer to assess their own work. Closed or leading questions ("You knew the deadline, didn't you?") make people defensive.

head: Situation
Best response
rows: Officer becomes defensive and blames colleagues
Stay calm, listen, acknowledge the feeling and return to the facts
Pause, offer a moment, do not rush, then continue gently
Check the evidence together; if you were wrong, say so
Officer is repeatedly late (for example, 30 minutes late for a shift)
Speak privately, state the facts and ask for the officer's view before drawing conclusions
Officer's work suddenly worsens and she seems stressed
Ask gently how she is and point her to support such as the employee assistance service or human resources

blocks.note: Do not mix praise and criticism so tightly that neither is heard. Be clear about the one or two points that matter most.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Coaching** uses questions to help an officer find the answer, rather than telling them what to do. The **GROW** model is a common structure.

head: Stage
Meaning
Sample question
rows: What do you want to achieve?
"What would a good result look like by June?"
"What is happening at the moment? What have you tried?"
"What choices do you have? What else?"
What will you do, and when?
"Which will you try first and by when?"

blocks.p: Telling is quicker, and right when there is danger or a clear rule. Coaching builds skill and ownership, and suits problems where the officer can find the solution.

sections.title: Recognising good work and closing performance gaps

blocks.p: Recognition shows officers that their effort is seen. It reinforces good behaviour so that it is repeated (**positive reinforcement**), shows the team what good work looks like and helps keep good staff, which matters in public bodies where pay rises are limited. Recognition does not need money.

head: Way to recognise
Example
rows: "Your reading club doubled visits by children, which brought many families into the library."
A letter or email copied to the officer's file
A line in the agency's newsletter or at a staff meeting
Representing the unit at a meeting, or a training place
Thanking the whole team when a deadline is met together

blocks.p: Make praise **specific** and **fair**. Praise that is general or repeated for everyone loses value. Do not reward only the people who are most visible.
When monitoring shows a gap between standard and performance, follow these steps in order.

flow: Check the evidence: which errors, how often, since when
Meet the officer privately to hear their view
Find the cause: skills, knowledge, resources, unclear instructions, workload, health or motivation
Agree the fix: coaching, training, a better tool or clearer instructions
Write an improvement plan with actions, support, dates and how progress will be checked
Review progress on the dates agreed and recognise improvement
If performance is still well below standard, follow the agency's formal procedure with human resource advice

head: Cause
Typical sign
Usual response
rows: New officer making errors in tender documents
Does not know what is expected
Different officers do the task differently
Good staff all struggling with a slow system
Report the problem, fix the resource
Sudden decline in a reliable officer
Ask gently, offer support, adjust temporarily if possible
Knows the standard, has had support and still does not meet it

ul: The specific gap, with facts
The standard that must be reached
Actions the officer will take
Support the manager will give (coaching, training, supervision)
Dates for review and the final date
How progress will be measured
The officer's comments, and signatures where the agency's procedure requires them

blocks.note: In the public service, formal action on poor performance must follow the agency's procedure and the public service rules, with the human resource unit involved. A manager should never skip steps or act on a single incident.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A brief record of each feedback meeting lets you **track progress** and keeps the facts clear if the matter arises later, for example in an appraisal, a grievance or a formal process. Memory is not enough.

ul: The date, who was present and the purpose
The facts discussed
The officer's views
The actions agreed, with dates and who will do what
The date of the next review

blocks.note: Write facts and agreed actions, not opinions about character. Imagine the officer reading the note.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Keep notes **securely**, with access limited to those who need them (for example in a locked cabinet or a password-protected folder).
Do not leave performance papers on a desk or on a shared drive.
Do not discuss one officer's performance with another. If an officer asks why a colleague was given an improvement plan, say politely that the matter is confidential to that person.
Use personal information only for its purpose, in line with the data protection law, and follow the agency's records policy.

blocks.p: Treat all officers by the same standards. Giving less feedback or fewer chances to improve to staff because of religion, gender, age, disability or any similar factor is unfair, breaks public service rules and may break the law. Raise any concern about a process with the human resource unit. Protect anyone who complains in good faith from bad treatment.

sections.title: Team performance, 360-degree feedback and reviewing the system

ul: **Share the team's overall figures** with all members each month, so that the team can see progress and solve problems together.
Set team targets as well as individual ones where the work is shared.
Hold short team meetings to look at results and causes, and ask for ideas.
Collect views from the public with a **short anonymous survey** after service, or comment cards, and share the results.
Do not compare officers in public in a way that shames them.

blocks.p: Many public agencies ask officers to complete a **self-assessment** before a review meeting. The officer reflects on achievements and difficulties, the manager gets a different view, and the discussion becomes two-way. Where views differ, check the evidence together.

**360-degree feedback** collects views on a manager or officer from their own manager, peers, staff they lead and sometimes clients. It shows blind spots, such as unclear instructions, that a single reviewer might miss.

head: Strength
Limit
rows: Takes time to collect and analyse
People may not be honest if they fear being identified
Can be used unfairly if not well explained

blocks.p: For best results: explain the purpose, keep replies anonymous (with enough respondents to protect identity), use it for development first and give support afterwards.

A manager who asks for feedback sets an example. If a senior officer tells you that your instructions are often unclear, do not defend or argue. **Thank him, ask for examples and agree a change.** Then follow it up. This builds trust and makes officers more willing to accept feedback themselves.

Monitoring itself needs review. If officers say that the monthly forms take hours and nothing is done with them, **review the forms with staff and keep only what is used**. A good system is simple, useful and trusted. Check at least once a year: Are the measures still relevant? Is the evidence reliable? Is anyone using the results? Are all staff treated the same way?

blocks.note: If you collect information and never use it, the team learns that monitoring is only paperwork.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: explain why targets and standards must be agreed, and write them in SMART form.
distinguish a duty, a performance standard, a target, a KPI and a baseline.
choose a balanced set of measures and a mix of monitoring methods.
build a simple monitoring plan with a timetable.
work out a percentage of target, an average, progress against an even pace and a percentage change, and check the data before acting.
explain when the cause of poor results is the process and not the person.
name the main rating errors and keep dated notes to avoid them.
give feedback using SBI: timely, specific, balanced and, for correction, private.
respond calmly when an officer is defensive, upset or stressed.
use the GROW model to coach.
recognise good work in specific, low-cost ways.
find the cause of a gap, agree an improvement plan and follow formal procedure when necessary.
keep brief, factual notes and store them securely, and keep other officers' matters confidential.
explain the uses of self-assessment and 360-degree feedback, and respond well to feedback on my own work.
review a monitoring system and keep only what is useful.

terms: Regular, fair checking of how well people and teams are doing against agreed expectations.
A stated level of quality, quantity or time for a task.
A specific result to be reached by a set date.
Key performance indicator: a measure used to track progress towards an important target.
A starting measurement used for later comparison.
One strong point colours the whole rating.
One weak point colours the whole rating downwards.
Recent events outweigh the rest of the review period.
Rating everyone in the middle to avoid high or low scores.
Information about performance, given so that it can improve.
Situation, Behaviour, Impact: a model for factual feedback.
Goal, Reality, Options, Way forward: a coaching model.
Praise or reward that makes good behaviour more likely to be repeated.
A written plan of actions, support and dates to bring performance up to standard.
An officer's own review of their performance, written before a review meeting.
Views collected from a person's manager, peers, staff and sometimes clients.
Keeping personal information private and sharing it only with those who need it.

c1.title: Building inspections in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: The building inspection unit of a municipal corporation in Savanna-la-Mar has six inspectors. The unit's target is for 90% of inspection requests to be completed within five working days. In May the unit received 240 requests and completed 192 within five working days. The unit head, Mrs Janelle Brown, has noticed that one inspector, Mr Dwayne Lewis, closed the most inspections but his reports are often missing the plot number.

c2.title: A registry unit in Spanish Town
c2.text: Mr Everton Samuels supervises a registry unit in a ministry in Spanish Town. Ms Shanice Bailey, a good officer, was late with two returns in October and made a figure error in one. When Mr Samuels met her, she said the new data-entry system freezes each afternoon and that two colleagues are on leave. Mr Samuels also remembers that Ms Bailey has been excellent all year, but the October errors are the most recent events and are fresh in his mind.

c3.title: Reviewing the forms at a health clinic office
c3.text: A regional health authority office in Mandeville asks its seven clerks to complete a 12-page monitoring form every week. Clerks say they have never seen any feedback from the forms. The office manager, Mr Orlando Gray, wants to improve monitoring before the next quarter. He also plans to send a short survey to patients and to introduce 360-degree feedback for the three senior clerks.

c4.title: Late reports in a parish office
c4.text: Mrs Nadine Powell leads a team of five officers at a government agency in Port Antonio. An officer, Mr Kemar Hall, has handed in four monthly reports late. Mrs Powell wants him to improve, and Mr Hall has said he does not fully understand the new report template. If his work does not improve after support, she must decide the next step. She also wants to thank another officer, Ms Monique Reid, who trained two new colleagues in her own time.

c5.title: Team target for the front counter
c5.text: A front counter team of eight at a ministry's customer centre in Half-Way Tree must serve 3,000 customers in a quarter. After the first two months it has served 1,900. The unit head, Mrs Sandra Pinnock, plans to share the figures at the monthly team meeting. A supervisor has said privately that an officer, Mr Rohan Clarke, is slow and that his performance must be 'dealt with' publicly.

questions.q: Mrs Brown wants to know whether the unit met its target in May. What percentage of requests were completed within five working days?
o: 80%, so the target was missed
80%, so the target was met
92%, so the target was met
20%, so the target was missed
questions.why: 192 ÷ 240 = 0.8, or 80%. The target was 90%, so it was missed. Always compare the result with the target before you conclude.

questions.q: The target was to complete 90% of the 240 requests on time. How many requests would that have been?
questions.why: 90% of 240 is 0.9 × 240 = 216. The unit completed 192, so it was 24 requests short.

questions.q: Mr Lewis closed the most inspections, but his reports often leave out the plot number. What should Mrs Brown do?
o: Praise him for his output, because quantity is the main measure
Reduce his workload at once so that fewer errors are likely to occur
Check a sample of his reports and discuss the omissions with him
Share his figures with the team as an example of poor work habits
questions.why: One measure can mislead. Output without quality is not good performance, so check a sample of his reports, then speak to him privately and agree how to fix the omissions.

questions.q: Mrs Brown wants a fair picture of each inspector's performance. Which mix of evidence is best?
o: Only the number of inspections that each inspector completes in a month
Comments from the other inspectors about how each colleague performs
The unit head's general impression formed over the course of the quarter
Inspection records, a sample of report checks and applicant feedback
questions.why: A mix of quantity, quality and client evidence gives a balanced picture. A single source, or an impression, is easy to distort.

questions.q: Mr Samuels rates Ms Bailey poorly on every criterion because of the October errors, forgetting the rest of the year. Which error is this?
o: Recency effect
Halo effect
Central tendency
Leniency bias
questions.why: The recent events are outweighing the whole period. Dated notes kept through the year help avoid this.

questions.q: What is the best way for Mr Samuels to avoid this error in future?
o: Ask officers to remember their own successes at review time
Keep short dated notes on each officer throughout the year
Rate only the last month in each quarter
Use the same rating for every officer to avoid disputes
questions.why: Dated notes give evidence from the whole period. Rating everyone the same is central tendency, which is also unfair.

questions.q: Ms Bailey explains that the system freezes each afternoon and two colleagues are on leave. What should Mr Samuels do first?
o: Record that she gave excuses and leave the rating unchanged for now
Move her to other work so that she has no further delays to explain
Check whether the system fault and shortage affected results
Ask her colleagues at a team meeting whether she is telling the truth
questions.why: A manager looks for the cause before judging. If the process or resources caused the delay, they must be fixed, and her rating should reflect the full facts.

questions.q: Mr Samuels meets Ms Bailey. Which opening is best for corrective feedback on the two late returns?
o: You were careless in October and it must not happen again this year.
Everyone knows the October returns were late, and I am very disappointed.
I will not discuss it now because you seem to have an excuse ready.
In October, two returns came in after the deadline. How do you see it?
questions.why: It states the situation and facts without judging character, and it invites her view. This is the SBI approach and keeps the talk two-way.

questions.q: The clerks say no feedback comes from the 12-page weekly form. What should Mr Gray do?
o: Review the form with the clerks and keep only what is used
Keep the form unchanged because completeness is most important
Ask clerks to complete the form faster and in less detail
Collect the forms but file them until the year-end appraisal
questions.why: A form that takes hours and produces no action teaches staff that monitoring is paperwork. Cut it down to what is useful and make sure the results are fed back.

questions.q: Mr Gray wants the clerks to see how the whole office is doing. What is the best approach?
o: Display each clerk's result on the wall with a ranking from top to bottom
Share overall figures monthly and discuss the causes together
Report the figures only to the regional director each quarter
Share the figures with the clerks only when a target has been missed
questions.why: Team figures help everyone see progress and solve problems together. Public ranking of individuals can shame staff and damage trust.

questions.q: Which survey approach is best for collecting views from patients about the clerks' service?
o: A long form sent to every patient once a year
A question asked by the clerk who has just served the patient
A short anonymous survey given after each service
Comments collected only from patients who complain
questions.why: A short anonymous survey is easy to complete and encourages honest replies. A long form has a low response, and asking face to face may produce flattering answers.

questions.q: For 360-degree feedback on the three senior clerks, who should give views?
o: Only the office manager, who knows their daily work the best
Only the clerks they supervise, to avoid any pressure from above
Only patients, because patients are the ones who receive the service
Their manager, peers, supervised clerks and sometimes patients
questions.why: 360-degree feedback uses several sources, to give a fuller picture and show blind spots. One group alone is not 360 degrees.

questions.q: Mr Hall has handed in four reports late and says he does not fully understand the template. What should Mrs Powell do first?
o: Find the cause with him and arrange coaching on the template
Issue a written warning now so that the problem is on record
Give the reports to another officer without discussing it with him
Remind the whole team in writing to read their templates carefully
questions.why: The cause is a skills or knowledge gap, so coaching or training is the first step. Formal action comes only after support has failed.

questions.q: Mrs Powell and Mr Hall agree a plan. Which plan is best?
o: Mr Hall will try harder to be on time with his monthly reports from now on
Coaching in week 1, a draft report by 25 November and a review on 15 December
Reports should be of a much better quality before the end of the working year
Mrs Powell will check Mr Hall's reports whenever she has some free time to do so
questions.why: A good plan has specific actions, support, dates and a way to check progress. The others are vague and cannot be reviewed.

questions.q: After coaching and support, Mr Hall's reports are still late and far below standard. What should Mrs Powell do next?
o: Stop giving him any reports and say nothing to him about it
Discuss his case with the other officers to get their views on it
Follow the agency's formal procedure with human resource advice
Lower the standard for his reports so that he is able to meet it
questions.why: Informal support has been tried, so the next step is the formal procedure, taken fairly and with HR guidance. Lowering the standard is unfair to others.

questions.q: Mrs Powell wants to recognise Ms Reid for training two new colleagues. Which is the best way?
o: A general 'well done' given in passing at the end of a long meeting
A reward given only if Ms Reid herself asks for recognition
A remark to her colleagues about how late she worked in her own time
Specific praise for what she did, with a written note for her file
questions.why: Specific praise tells her what was valued, and a written note adds lasting recognition. General praise is less meaningful.

questions.q: The team must serve 3,000 customers in a quarter, evenly. After two months it has served 1,900. How far ahead or behind is it?
o: 100 behind
100 ahead
1,100 behind
700 ahead
questions.why: After two of three months, the even pace is 2,000. The team has served 1,900, so it is 100 behind and can still catch up with a small increase.

questions.q: The supervisor says Mr Clarke is slow and should be 'dealt with' publicly. What should Mrs Pinnock do?
o: Name him at the monthly team meeting as an example to others
Check his figures and discuss them with him in private
Ask the other officers to comment on his speed of working
Move him to the back office without any discussion with him
questions.why: Corrective feedback should be based on facts and given privately. Public shaming harms trust and may be unfair if the cause is not known.

questions.q: Mrs Pinnock finds the team misses its target while every officer is busy. Files wait for a signature between steps. What is the most likely cause?
o: A lack of effort from the officers working at the counter
Officers who are poor at meeting their individual targets
The way the work flows between the steps of the process
Too few client surveys being completed by customers
questions.why: If everyone is busy and files wait between steps, the process is the likely problem. Map the steps, measure waiting and remove the delay.

questions.q: A manager receives feedback from an experienced officer that her instructions are often unclear. What is the best response?
o: Explain that her instructions are always clear
Ask other officers whether they agree before replying
Note it, but take no action until the appraisal
Thank him, ask for examples and agree a change
questions.why: Welcoming feedback shows that feedback is normal and two-way, and examples let her improve. It also encourages others to accept feedback.
